{{Short description|Three-dimensional orthogonal coordinate system}}
[[File:Parabolic_coordinates_3D.png|thumb|alt=Parabolic coordinates 3D|Parabolic coordinates 3D]]
'''Paraboloidal coordinates''' are three-dimensional [[orthogonal coordinates]] <math>(\mu, \nu, \lambda)</math> that generalize two-dimensional [[parabolic coordinates]]. They possess elliptic [[paraboloids]] as one-coordinate surfaces. As such, they should be distinguished from [[parabolic cylindrical coordinates]] and [[Parabolic_coordinates#Three-dimensional_parabolic_coordinates|parabolic rotational coordinates]], both of which are also generalizations of two-dimensional parabolic coordinates. The coordinate surfaces of the former are parabolic cylinders, and the coordinate surfaces of the latter are ''circular'' paraboloids.

Differently from cylindrical and rotational parabolic coordinates, but similarly to the related [[ellipsoidal coordinates]], the coordinate surfaces of the paraboloidal coordinate system are ''not'' produced by rotating or projecting any two-dimensional orthogonal coordinate system.

==Basic formulas==

The Cartesian coordinates <math>(x, y, z)</math> can be produced from the ellipsoidal coordinates 
<math>(\mu, \nu, \lambda)</math> by the equations<ref name="Voon2011">{{Citation
| last1  = Yoon
| first1 = LCLY
| last2  = M
| first2 = Willatzen
| title     = Separable Boundary-Value Problems in Physics
| publisher = Wiley-VCH
| year    = 2011
| isbn    = 978-3-527-63492-7
| page    =  217
}}</ref>

:<math>
x^{2} = \frac{4}{b-c}(\mu - b)(b - \nu)(b - \lambda)
</math>

:<math>
y^{2} = \frac{4}{b-c}(\mu - c)(c - \nu)(\lambda - c)
</math>

:<math>
z = \mu + \nu + \lambda - b - c
</math>

with

:<math>
\mu > b > \lambda > c > \nu > 0
</math>

Consequently, surfaces of constant <math>\mu</math> are downward opening elliptic paraboloids:

:<math>
\frac{x^2}{\mu - b} + \frac{y^2}{\mu - c} = -4 (z - \mu)
</math>

Similarly, surfaces of constant <math>\nu</math> are ''upward'' opening elliptic paraboloids,

:<math>
\frac{x^2}{b - \nu} + \frac{y^2}{c - \nu} = 4 (z - \nu)
</math>

whereas surfaces of constant <math>\lambda</math> are hyperbolic paraboloids:

:<math>
\frac{x^2}{b - \lambda} - \frac{y^2}{\lambda - c} = 4 (z - \lambda)
</math>

==Scale factors==

The scale factors for the paraboloidal coordinates <math>(\mu, \nu, \lambda)</math> are<ref>Willatzen and Yoon (2011), p. 219</ref>

:<math>
h_{\mu} = \left[ \frac{\left(\mu - \nu \right) \left(\mu - \lambda \right)}{ \left(\mu - b \right) \left(\mu - c \right)} \right]^{1/2}
</math>

:<math>
h_{\nu} = \left[\frac{\left(\mu - \nu \right) \left( \lambda - \nu \right)}{ \left(b - \nu \right) \left(c - \nu \right)} \right]^{1/2}
</math>

:<math>
h_{\lambda} = \left[\frac{\left(\lambda - \nu \right) \left(\mu - \lambda \right)}{ \left(b - \lambda \right) \left(\lambda - c \right)} \right]^{1/2}
</math>

Hence, the [[infinitesimal]] [[volume element]] is

:<math>
dV = \frac{(\mu - \nu)(\mu - \lambda)(\lambda - \nu)}{\left[(\mu - b)(\mu - c)(b - \nu)(c - \nu)(b - \lambda)(\lambda - c) \right]^{1/2}} \  d\lambda d\mu d\nu
</math>

== Differential operators ==

Common differential operators can be expressed in the coordinates <math>(\mu, \nu, \lambda)</math> by substituting the scale factors into the [[Orthogonal_coordinates#Differential_operators_in_three_dimensions|general formulas for these operators]], which are applicable to any three-dimensional orthogonal coordinates. For instance, the [[gradient operator]] is

:<math>
\nabla = \left[\frac{ \left(\mu - b \right) \left(\mu - c \right)}{\left(\mu - \nu \right) \left(\mu - \lambda \right)} \right]^{1/2} \mathbf{e}_{\mu} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} + \left[\frac{\left(b - \nu \right) \left(c - \nu \right)}{\left(\mu - \nu \right) \left( \lambda - \nu \right)} \right]^{1/2} \mathbf{e}_{\nu} \frac{\partial}{\partial \nu} + \left[\frac{\left(b - \lambda \right) \left(\lambda - c \right)}{\left(\lambda - \nu \right) \left(\mu - \lambda \right)} \right]^{1/2} \mathbf{e}_{\lambda} \frac{\partial}{\partial \lambda}
</math>

and the [[Laplacian]] is

:<math>
\begin{align}
\nabla^2 = &\left[\frac{ \left(\mu - b \right) \left(\mu - c \right)}{\left(\mu - \nu \right) \left(\mu - \lambda \right)} \right]^{1/2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \left[(\mu - b)^{1/2}(\mu - c)^{1/2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \right] \\ 
&+ \left[\frac{\left(b - \nu \right) \left(c - \nu \right)}{\left(\mu - \nu \right) \left( \lambda - \nu \right)} \right]^{1/2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \nu} \left[ (b - \nu)^{1/2}(c - \nu)^{1/2}\frac{\partial}{\partial \nu} \right] \\
&+ \left[\frac{\left(b - \lambda \right) \left(\lambda - c \right)}{\left(\lambda - \nu \right) \left(\mu - \lambda \right)} \right]^{1/2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \lambda} \left[(b - \lambda)^{1/2}(\lambda -c)^{1/2} \frac{\partial}{\partial \lambda} \right]
\end{align}
</math>

== Applications ==

Paraboloidal coordinates can be useful for solving certain [[partial differential equations]]. For instance, the [[Laplace equation]] and [[Helmholtz equation]] are both [[Separable partial differential equation|separable]] in paraboloidal coordinates. Hence, the coordinates can be used to solve these equations in geometries with paraboloidal symmetry, i.e. with boundary conditions specified on sections of paraboloids.

The Helmholtz equation is <math>(\nabla^2  + k^2) \psi = 0</math>. Taking <math>\psi = M(\mu)N(\nu)\Lambda(\lambda)</math>, the separated equations are<ref>Willatzen and Yoon (2011), p. 227</ref>

:<math>
\begin{align}
&(\mu - b)(\mu - c) \frac{d^2M}{d\mu^2} + \frac{1}{2}\left[2 \mu - (b + c) \right] \frac{dM}{d\mu} + \left[k^2 \mu^2 + \alpha_3 \mu - \alpha_2\right] M = 0 \\
&(b - \nu)(c - \nu) \frac{d^2N}{d\nu^2} + \frac{1}{2}\left[2 \nu - (b + c) \right] \frac{dN}{d\nu} + \left[k^2 \nu^2 + \alpha_3 \nu - \alpha_2\right] N = 0 \\
&(b - \lambda)(\lambda - c) \frac{d^2\Lambda}{d\lambda^2} - \frac{1}{2}\left[2 \lambda - (b + c) \right] \frac{d\Lambda}{d\lambda} - \left[k^2 \lambda^2 + \alpha_3 \lambda - \alpha_2\right] \Lambda = 0 \\
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>\alpha_2</math> and <math>\alpha_3</math> are the two separation constants. Similarly, the separated equations for the Laplace equation can be obtained by setting <math>k = 0</math> in the above.

Each of the separated equations can be cast in the form of the [[Baer equation]]. Direct solution of the equations is difficult, however, in part because the separation constants <math>\alpha_2</math> and <math>\alpha_3</math> appear simultaneously in all three equations. 

Following the above approach, paraboloidal coordinates have been used to solve for the [[electric field]] surrounding a [[Electrical conductor|conducting]] paraboloid.<ref name="Duggen2012">{{Citation
| last1       = Duggen
| first1      = L
| last2       = Willatzen
| first2      = M
| last3       = Voon
| first3      = L C Lew Yan
| year       = 2012
| title      = Laplace boundary-value problem in paraboloidal coordinates
| journal    =European Journal of Physics
| volume     = 33
| issue      = 3
| pages      = 689–696
| doi      = 10.1088/0143-0807/33/3/689
| bibcode = 2012EJPh...33..689D
}}</ref>
